The early life stages of Senegalese hake are characterised by a remarkably small initial mass; newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from pelagic eggs measuring approximately 900 micrometers in diameter and weigh just 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture. This minute size, typical of many merlucciids, reflects a strategy of high fecundity coupled with minimal maternal investment per offspring. Following a brief endotrophic period during which the larvae rely on endogenous yolk reserves, the onset of exogenous feeding occurs once the mouth gapes open and retinal differentiation permits prey detection. The juveniles then embark on a rapid growth trajectory that continues throughout the sub-adult phase. Field surveys indicate that the maximum body length attained by adults in the population reaches 81 centimeters [Li = 81 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range reported for the genus Merluccius in West African waters. This substantial ultimate total length situates the species as one of the larger hakes in the eastern Atlantic, though individuals rarely achieve this maximum under heavy fishing pressure.

Sexual maturation in female Senegalese hake is closely tied to both body size and local thermal conditions. A comprehensive analysis of ovarian development across multiple cohorts determined that the total length at puberty for females is 37 centimeters [Lp = 37 centimeters], corresponding to the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence. This length threshold, which typically falls within a range of 33 to 39 centimeters depending on nutritional history and population density, marks the transition from an immature, non-reproductive state to a reproductively viable one. The corresponding somatic investment required to reach this developmental milestone is substantial; weight-length regressions derived from specimen collections indicate that females attain a wet weight at puberty of approximately 363 grams [Wwp = approximately 363 grams] by the time they first become capable of spawning. This value represents the point at which energy reserves are sufficient to support the metabolic demands of gamete production, a critical prerequisite for successful reproduction in a species that spawns multiple times over its life span.

Adult body size in Senegalese hake displays a strong allometric relationship with mass, and the ultimate wet weight predicted from the species length-mass power function is 4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams] for an individual reaching the asymptotic length of 81 centimeters. This maximum recorded body mass, derived from the equation relating total length to eviscerated weight, places the species in an intermediate position among Atlantic hakes, heavier than the smaller Merluccius merluccius from the Mediterranean but considerably lighter than the giant Merluccius australis from the Southern Hemisphere. The reproductive output of mature females scales accordingly, with gravid individuals carrying substantial ovarian masses prior to spawning. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) peaks during the main spawning season and reaches approximately 25% [GSI = approximately 25%] when measured at a stable water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. Such a high index underscores the considerable energetic allocation toward egg production in this batch-spawning species.

Lifespan estimates for Senegalese hake, derived from otolith-based age readings of wild-caught individuals, indicate that the maximum recorded longevity under natural thermal conditions is approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] at a mean annual water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This figure, equivalent to roughly two decades, positions the species as a moderately long-lived teleost within the Gadiformes, with a life span that allows for multiple reproductive seasons. The extended duration of the adult phase is ecologically significant, as it permits iteroparous spawning over many years, buffering the population against years of poor recruitment. In comparison to the congeneric European hake Merluccius merluccius, which rarely exceeds 15 years in the wild, the Senegalese hake appears to exhibit a slightly slower pace of life, possibly reflecting the cooler, more stable upwelling environment of the Canary Current Large Marine Ecosystem where it predominantly resides.

The remarkable growth trajectory of Senegalese hake, from a pelagic larva weighing only 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams] to an adult exceeding 4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams], is supported by the high productivity of the Mauritanian-Senegalese continental shelf. The length at which females initiate vitellogenesis, 37 centimeters [Lp = 37 centimeters], corresponds to a mass of approximately 363 grams [Wwp = approximately 363 grams], roughly nine percent of the ultimate adult mass. The gonadosomatic index reaches 25% [GSI = 25%] under the prevailing thermal conditions of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. The entire life cycle, from pelagic egg to senescent adult, spans approximately 7300 days [am = approximately 7300 days] at the same thermal regime of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], completing a life history strategy finely tuned to the predictable seasonal upwelling patterns off Northwest Africa.
